nodeData.note: Beginner track · What AI is, its history, the kinds of AI, how machines learn, myths and limits.

children.note: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that do tasks we normally link with human thinking, such as recognising speech, spotting patterns or writing text. This map explains what it is, how it differs from ordinary software, and where you already use it.
AI has a seventy-year story of big hopes, hard disappointments and sudden breakthroughs. Knowing the pattern helps you judge today's excitement calmly.
AI comes in several kinds, sorted in different ways: by how broad it is, by how it gets its rules, by how it learns, and by what it produces. This map lays out the main labels in plain words.
Machines learn by looking at many examples, making guesses, measuring their mistakes and adjusting, over and over. This map walks through that loop in plain words, with everyday analogies.
AI is powerful but far from magic. This map separates common myths from reality and explains the main limits: made-up answers, bias, understanding, jobs, energy and what AI still cannot do.
AI is changing many jobs and creating some new ones. This map explains the main AI roles, how AI helps people in ordinary professions, the skills to build, free ways to learn, and traps to avoid.

nodeData.note: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that do tasks we normally link with human thinking, such as recognising speech, spotting patterns or writing text. This map explains what it is, how it differs from ordinary software, and where you already use it.

children.note: AI is a broad label, not one single machine. It covers many methods that let computers handle tasks that once needed a person's judgement.
AI is the ability of a computer system to do things we associate with human intelligence: learning, reasoning, understanding language, seeing and deciding.

manas.q: In one sentence, what is artificial intelligence?

children.topic: It is a field and a tool
children.note: The word is used both for a branch of computer science (the research) and for the products it creates, such as a chatbot or a photo-sorting app.
The American computer scientist John McCarthy proposed the name 'artificial intelligence' for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the USA.

manas.q: Which 1956 event gave AI its name as a field?

children.note: Today's AI can be excellent at one job, such as translating Swahili to English, and useless at another. It is not a general mind like a person's.
Once a task becomes routine for computers, such as spell-checking or route-finding, people often stop calling it AI. The label keeps moving to the newest, hardest tasks.
Most AI is invisible software running on phones and servers. Robots are machines with bodies; some use AI, many do not.
The key difference is how the instructions are made: written by hand, or learned from examples.
In a normal program, a person writes every step: 'if the balance is below zero, show a warning'. The computer does exactly that and nothing more.

manas.q: How does ordinary software decide what to do?

children.note: With machine learning, people give the computer many examples and it works out its own pattern, for example which emails are spam.

manas.q: What is the big difference between ordinary software and machine learning?

children.note: Ordinary software is like a recipe card followed word for word. Learning software is like an apprentice cook who watches thousands of dishes and picks up the knack.
Some tasks are too fuzzy to write rules for. Nobody can list every rule for recognising a face or a cat, but a system can learn it from many photos.
Because the system learned its own rules, it can make odd mistakes and it is often hard to explain exactly why it gave a particular answer.
Ordinary programs give the same output for the same input. Many AI chatbots add a little randomness, so the same question can get different wording each time.
Three plain words explain most modern AI: the examples it learns from, the pattern-holder it builds, and the practice that builds it.
Data is the collection of examples a system learns from: photos, sentences, prices, X-rays, sounds. More varied, accurate data usually means a better system.

manas.q: In AI, what is 'data'?

children.note: A model is the stored result of learning, a large set of numbers that captures patterns from the data. You feed it new input and it produces an output.

manas.q: What is an AI 'model'?

children.note: Training is the process of showing the model examples, checking its guesses and nudging its numbers until the guesses improve.

manas.q: What happens during training?

children.note: After training, the model is put to work on new cases it has never seen. This stage is often called inference, or simply using the model.
A new conductor learns which stops are busy by riding the route for weeks (training). Later he predicts crowds on a new day (using the model), sometimes wrongly.
If the examples are wrong, missing or one-sided, the model learns the wrong lessons. Good data matters as much as clever methods.

manas.q: Why does the quality of data matter so much?

children.note: Most people use AI many times a day without noticing it.
Face unlock, the keyboard that suggests your next word, photo search ('show me beach pictures') and voice typing all rely on learned patterns.
Navigation apps estimate traffic and arrival times by learning from the movement of many phones on the road.
Banks and mobile-money services use pattern-spotting systems to flag unusual transactions that may be fraud, then ask a human to check.
Spam filters learn what junk mail looks like and move it out of your inbox. They were one of the earliest everyday uses of machine learning.
Video, music and shopping apps suggest what to watch, hear or buy next by learning from what you and similar people chose before.
Translation tools can turn English into Swahili, Hindi and many other languages, and voice assistants convert speech to text.
Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini answer questions and draft text. They are one kind of AI, not the whole of it.
AI tools help read some medical scans and photos of crop leaves to flag possible disease. A trained person should still make the final decision.

children.topic: A chatbot answer, step by step
children.note: A look inside one everyday AI tool, using only plain words.
Your question is split into small pieces of text called tokens, roughly word parts, which the model can handle as numbers.
The model guesses the most fitting next token, adds it, and repeats, building the answer one piece at a time.

manas.q: How does a chatbot build its answer?

children.note: It is not searching a stored copy of the internet. It draws on patterns learned in training, which is why it can be fluent yet wrong.
Some chatbots can also run a web search or read a file you upload, then use that text in their answer.
Makers add further training and checks so the tool refuses harmful requests and follows instructions more reliably.

children.topic: What AI is good and bad at
children.note: Knowing the strengths and weak spots helps you use AI wisely.
AI shines when there are many examples and a clear pattern: sorting photos, transcribing speech, flagging unusual payments.
A trained model can check millions of items in the time a person checks a few, which is why it is used for spam and fraud screening.
When something is unlike its training examples, AI can fail badly and confidently.

manas.q: When is AI most likely to fail?

children.note: AI lacks the everyday life experience people use to notice that an answer is silly or dangerous.
Chatbots can produce fluent but false statements. Always verify important facts, figures and references.
AI suggests; humans decide. In medicine, law, money and safety, a qualified person should review AI output.
A small glossary for reading news and articles about AI.
The part of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being given every rule by hand.

manas.q: What is machine learning?

children.note: Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It powers modern speech, image and language tools.
A model loosely inspired by brain cells: many simple connected units whose connection strengths are adjusted during training.

manas.q: What is a neural network, in plain words?

children.note: AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio or code, rather than only sorting or predicting.

manas.q: What makes AI 'generative'?

children.note: A model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. It is the engine inside most chatbots.

manas.q: What is a large language model?

children.note: A step-by-step method for solving a problem. Learning algorithms are the methods used to train models.
The instruction or question you type into a generative AI tool.
Short, trusted videos that explain the basics.

3Blue1Brown's gentle visual tour of how chatbots predict words.

nodeData.note: AI has a seventy-year story of big hopes, hard disappointments and sudden breakthroughs. Knowing the pattern helps you judge today's excitement calmly.

children.note: Long before computers, people imagined thinking machines. The modern story starts with a few mathematicians in the 1940s and 1950s.
Myths and stories in many cultures describe statues, dolls or servants brought to life by skilled makers. The wish for thinking machines is very old.
A British mathematician who helped found computer science and worked on breaking wartime codes. He asked seriously whether machines could think.

manas.q: Which British mathematician is often called a father of AI and computer science?

children.note: In his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Turing suggested judging a machine by whether its typed conversation could pass for a person's.

manas.q: What did Turing propose in his 1950 paper?

children.note: It shifted the question from 'can machines think?' to 'can they behave in a way we cannot tell apart from a person?'. Critics say fooling people is not the same as understanding.
Machines built in the 1940s showed that calculation could be automated, which made people wonder what else could be.
AI became a named research field in 1956 and enjoyed two decades of bold optimism.
A summer workshop at Dartmouth College, USA, organised by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, is seen as AI's founding event.

manas.q: Where and when is AI usually said to have been founded as a field?

children.note: Presented around the Dartmouth workshop by Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, it proved maths theorems using hand-written logical steps.
Frank Rosenblatt built an early learning machine inspired by brain cells. It was an ancestor of today's neural networks.
Joseph Weizenbaum's simple chat program at MIT imitated a therapist by rephrasing what people typed. Many users felt understood, which surprised and worried him.
Leading researchers predicted human-level machines within a generation. Real problems such as vision and common sense proved far harder.
Periods of hype were followed by cuts in money and interest, called AI winters.
A period when funding and enthusiasm for AI drop sharply after promises are not met.

manas.q: What is an 'AI winter'?

children.note: Slow progress and critical reviews, including the UK's 1973 Lighthill report, led governments to cut AI research funding.
Programs packed with if–then rules written with human experts, for example to suggest diagnoses or configure computers. They were the first big commercial AI.

manas.q: How did expert systems work?

children.note: A Stanford expert system from the 1970s that suggested treatments for blood infections using a few hundred rules. It was studied but not used routinely in hospitals.
Rule systems were costly to build, broke on cases nobody foresaw and could not learn. Upkeep became a burden.
When expert systems disappointed and special AI computers lost their market, funding fell again.
In 1986 Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularised backpropagation, a way to train layered neural networks, laying groundwork for later success.
Researchers shifted from hand-written rules to systems that learn patterns from data, helped by faster computers and the internet.
IBM's chess computer defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in New York, using massive search rather than learning.

manas.q: What happened in 1997 between IBM's Deep Blue and Garry Kasparov?

children.note: Spam filters, search engines and speech recognition improved by learning from data, often quietly behind the scenes.
Billions of web pages, photos and clicks gave learning systems far more examples than ever before.
A huge labelled photo collection led by Fei-Fei Li, with over 14 million images. From 2010 it hosted a yearly image-recognition contest.
Layered neural networks trained on graphics chips began to beat older methods, sparking today's boom.
A neural network by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton won the ImageNet contest by a wide margin, a turning point for deep learning.

manas.q: Which 2012 result is seen as the start of the deep learning boom?

children.note: Chips designed for video games turned out to be ideal for training neural networks fast, cutting weeks of work to days.
DeepMind's AlphaGo beat top Go player Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul in March 2016. Go had long been seen as too hard for computers.

manas.q: What did AlphaGo achieve in 2016?

children.note: Google researchers introduced the transformer design, which handles words in parallel and pays 'attention' to the most relevant ones. It underpins modern chatbots.

manas.q: What 2017 invention powers most modern language AI?

children.note: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformers learned language by predicting the next word in huge amounts of text.
Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun shared the 2018 Turing Award, computing's top honour, for their work on deep learning.
DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the 3D shapes of proteins with high accuracy, a long-standing problem in biology.
Chatbots brought AI to hundreds of millions of people and set off a race in investment, products and regulation.
OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. It reached about 100 million monthly users in two months.

manas.q: When was ChatGPT released, and how fast did it grow?

children.note: Others released chatbots and models, such as Claude, Gemini, Llama and DeepSeek. Several Chinese firms favour open-weights models anyone can download.
In November 2023 the UK hosted the first global AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, producing the Bletchley Declaration on shared risks.
In May 2023 Geoffrey Hinton left Google, saying he wanted to speak freely about the risks of AI.
The European Union's AI Act took effect on 1 August 2024, with duties phased in over several years by level of risk. Check the current text for details.

manas.q: When did the EU AI Act enter into force?

children.note: The Physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for neural network foundations. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the Chemistry prize for protein structure prediction.

manas.q: Which AI pioneers received Nobel prizes in 2024?

children.note: New models were trained to work through problems step by step before answering, improving results in maths, logic and coding.
Companies began offering 'agents' that take actions, such as browsing or filling in tasks, over longer periods. Their reliability is still being tested.
ChatGPT reported about 900 million weekly users in February 2026, and chip makers became some of the world's most valuable companies.
Debates now cover energy use, copyright, deepfakes, jobs, concentration of power and long-term safety.
Africa is building its own AI community, though most large models are still made elsewhere.
Launched in 2017 in South Africa, this yearly gathering builds machine learning skills across the continent and has spread through local IndabaX events.

manas.q: What is the Deep Learning Indaba?

children.note: Kenya's Data Protection Act of 2019 created the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, which matters for any AI using personal data. Check the current text.
Many African languages have little digital text, so AI tools often work worse in them. Collecting good local data is an active effort.
The past gives useful habits for reading today's headlines.
Each era promised human-level AI soon; each time, progress was real but slower and narrower than claimed.

manas.q: What repeated pattern does AI history show?

children.note: Big jumps came when more data and faster chips met a good idea, as in 2012 and after 2017.
Neural networks were out of fashion for years before becoming dominant. Ideas can be early rather than wrong.
Videos that tell the story well.

nodeData.note: AI comes in several kinds, sorted in different ways: by how broad it is, by how it gets its rules, by how it learns, and by what it produces. This map lays out the main labels in plain words.

children.note: There is no single family tree. People group AI by different questions, so one tool can carry several labels at once.
Narrow AI does one kind of task; general AI would handle almost any thinking task. Every AI in use today is narrow.

children.topic: Where do its rules come from?
children.note: Rule-based AI follows rules people wrote; learning AI finds its own patterns from examples.
Learning AI is usually trained with labelled examples, unlabelled examples, or rewards and penalties.
Predictive AI gives a label, number or choice; generative AI creates new text, images, sound or code.
A chatbot is narrow, learning-based, mostly trained on unlabelled text then refined with feedback, and generative.
The most important distinction for understanding headlines about AI.
AI built for a specific job, such as recognising faces, translating text or playing chess. Also called weak AI.

manas.q: What is narrow AI?

children.note: Even very capable chatbots are narrow in the sense that they lack reliable common sense, real-world experience and steady judgement outside their training.
Spam filters, voice typing, crop-disease photo apps, credit scoring and route planners each do one family of tasks well.
A hypothetical AI that could match or beat people across almost all thinking tasks and transfer skills to new problems.

manas.q: What does AGI stand for, and what would it be?

children.note: A further hypothetical stage where AI would far exceed the best humans in nearly every field. It does not exist.
Narrow AI is like a world-class chess player who cannot boil an egg. AGI would be an all-rounder who could learn any job.
Two broad approaches to making a machine act intelligently.
People write explicit if–then rules, such as 'if fever and stiff neck, flag meningitis risk'. It is the classic form of symbolic AI, as used in expert systems.

manas.q: How does rule-based AI work?

children.note: Rules are clear, predictable and easy to explain, which suits tax forms, eligibility checks and safety interlocks.

manas.q: When are hand-written rules a good choice?

children.note: Rules break when the world is messy. Nobody can write rules for every accent, handwriting style or photo angle.
The system is shown many examples and adjusts itself until its outputs match. Machine learning and deep learning are of this kind.

manas.q: How does learning AI get its rules?

children.note: It copes with fuzzy, varied tasks like speech, images and language that resist hand-written rules.
It needs lots of good data, can absorb bias and is often hard to explain.
Real products often combine both: a learned model makes a guess and fixed rules block unsafe or illegal actions.
Learning AI is usually trained in one of three styles, or a mix of them.
Learning from examples that come with the right answers attached, like flashcards with the answer on the back.

manas.q: What is supervised learning?

children.note: Thousands of emails each marked 'spam' or 'not spam' teach a filter to sort new mail.
Leaf photos labelled 'healthy' or by disease name train an app to flag problems in a farmer's field.
Someone must label every example, which takes time and money, and mistakes in labels teach mistakes.
Learning from examples with no answers attached; the system looks for groups and patterns on its own.

manas.q: What is unsupervised learning?

children.note: A shop's sales records can be grouped into similar kinds of buyers without anyone defining the groups first.
Spotting transactions that look unlike all the others can help catch fraud or faulty machines.
Like sorting a basket of unfamiliar fruit by colour and size, without knowing their names.
Learning by trial and error: the system tries actions and gets rewards or penalties, slowly finding what works.

manas.q: What is reinforcement learning?

children.note: AlphaGo improved partly by playing huge numbers of games against itself and learning from wins and losses.
Robots can learn to walk or grip by trying moves and being rewarded for progress, often first in simulation.
Like teaching a dog with treats: good actions are rewarded, so they happen more often.
Chatbots are often refined with human ratings of their answers, a form of reinforcement learning from human feedback.

manas.q: How are chatbots refined after their first training?

children.note: A useful split for everyday tools: does it judge, or does it create?
Gives a label, score or forecast, such as 'fraud likely', 'rain tomorrow' or 'this X-ray needs review'.

manas.q: What does predictive AI produce?

children.note: Creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or code, in response to a prompt.

manas.q: What does generative AI produce?

children.note: Large language models, inside chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, write and summarise text.
Other models make pictures, music or voices from a description, which also makes convincing fakes possible.
Both kinds learn patterns from data. Generative models use those patterns to produce something new instead of picking a label.
For a yes/no or number decision, predictive tools are usually simpler and easier to check. Generative tools suit drafting and brainstorming.
Common terms in news and product descriptions.
Learning AI built from neural networks with many layers. It powers most modern image, speech and language tools.

manas.q: What is deep learning?

children.note: AI that works with images and video, such as reading number plates or checking scans.
AI that works with human language: translation, speech-to-text, summaries and chat.
Machines that sense and move in the physical world. Some use AI for seeing and planning; many use fixed programs.
Systems that take a series of actions toward a goal, like searching, clicking and filling forms, not just answering once.

manas.q: What is an AI agent?

children.note: Models whose learned numbers are published so anyone can download and run them, unlike models only offered as an online service.
Whether and when general AI might arrive is one of the most argued questions in the field.
Several AI company leaders say AGI could come within years and have made it their stated goal.
Many researchers argue current methods lack real understanding, reliable reasoning and grounding in the physical world.
People disagree on what would count as AGI, so claims that it is near or far are hard to test.

manas.q: Why is it hard to say when AGI will arrive?

children.note: Some experts call reducing extreme risks from advanced AI a global priority; others think near-term harms like bias and misuse matter more.
Treat confident predictions in either direction with care, and judge tools by what they reliably do today.

nodeData.note: Machines learn by looking at many examples, making guesses, measuring their mistakes and adjusting, over and over. This map walks through that loop in plain words, with everyday analogies.

children.note: Learning means getting better at a task through experience rather than being told every step.
Instead of writing rules, we show the machine many examples and let it find the pattern that links inputs to outputs.

manas.q: What does it mean for a machine to 'learn'?

children.note: A child is not given a definition of a dog; they see many dogs, get corrected sometimes, and soon recognise new ones.

children.topic: The learning loop in one line
children.note: Show examples, let the model guess, measure the error, adjust, and repeat until the guesses are good enough.

manas.q: What are the steps of the basic learning loop?

children.note: The machine finds statistical patterns. It does not know what a dog is in the way a child comes to know it.
Learning only counts if the system does well on examples it has never seen, not just on the ones it practised with.

manas.q: What is the real test of whether a machine has learned?

children.note: Everything starts with data: the examples the machine will learn from.
Photos, sentences, sound clips, sales records, sensor readings, medical images: anything that can be stored as numbers.
For many tasks each example has an input (a leaf photo) and an answer, called a label (the disease name).

manas.q: What is a 'label' in machine learning?

children.note: Simple tasks may need hundreds of examples; recognising speech or writing text needs millions or far more.
Examples should cover the real range: different lighting, accents, ages, regions and devices.
To spot a maize leaf disease, you would collect many photos of healthy and sick leaves from different farms, seasons and phones.
Before training, people remove duplicates, fix errors and check labels. This unglamorous work often takes most of a project's time.
Data about people should be collected lawfully and fairly. In Kenya the Data Protection Act applies; check the current text.
A model is a pattern-holder with many adjustable settings. At first those settings are random, so its guesses are poor.
A large set of numbers arranged so that an input goes in and a prediction comes out. Training sets those numbers.

manas.q: What is a model, in plain words?

children.note: Imagine a mixing desk with millions of knobs. Each knob slightly changes the output; learning means turning them to the right positions.
A common kind of model made of layers of simple units. Each unit combines signals from the previous layer and passes a result on.
The clues a model uses, such as colour patches or word endings. Modern models discover useful clues by themselves.

manas.q: What are 'features' in machine learning?

children.note: Training is a loop: guess, measure the error, nudge the settings, repeat.
After each guess, the system compares its answer with the correct one and scores how wrong it was.

manas.q: How does a learning system know it made a mistake?

children.note: It then adjusts its settings a tiny step in the direction that would have made the error smaller.
This loop runs over all the examples, often many rounds, until the guesses stop improving much.
Like finding the bottom of a valley in fog by always stepping a little downhill. You get lower without seeing the whole map.
You wobble, notice which way you are falling, correct slightly, and after many tries balance without thinking.
Big models need special chips and lots of electricity because the loop runs billions of times.
Before trusting a model, we test it on examples it has never seen.
Data is split: most is used for practice (training set) and a held-back part checks real skill (test set).

manas.q: Why is data split into training and test sets?

children.note: If a student sees the exact exam questions in advance, a high score proves nothing. Test examples must stay hidden during training.
A model that memorises its training examples, including their noise, does well in practice but badly on new cases.

manas.q: What is overfitting?

children.note: A model too simple for the task misses the real pattern and does badly on both old and new examples.

children.topic: Test where it will be used
children.note: A model tested only in Nairobi hospitals may not perform the same in a rural clinic with different machines and patients.
The world changes, such as new fraud tricks or new diseases, so models must be monitored and retrained.
A model can only be as good as the examples it learned from.
Wrong, messy or missing data leads to wrong lessons, however clever the method.

manas.q: What does 'garbage in, garbage out' mean for AI?

children.note: If some sick leaves are labelled healthy, the model learns to miss that disease.
If a skin-condition tool saw mostly light-skinned patients, it may work worse on darker skin. Gaps in data become gaps in performance.

manas.q: How can missing groups in data cause harm?

children.note: Data from the past can carry past unfairness, for example in who got loans, and a model may copy it.
Models sometimes latch onto a side clue, such as a hospital's label on an X-ray, rather than the real sign of disease.
Collect varied data, check labels, test on different groups and involve people who know the setting.
Large language models follow the same loop at enormous scale, with extra stages.
The model is trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word piece. This is called pre-training.

manas.q: What is a language model trained to do during pre-training?

children.note: It is then trained on examples of helpful answers so it follows instructions instead of just continuing text.
People rate answers and the model is adjusted toward the preferred ones.
A chatbot does not learn from each chat by itself. Its knowledge is mostly fixed until its makers train a new version.

manas.q: Does a chatbot keep learning from every conversation?

children.topic: Why it can be out of date
children.note: Because training ends on a certain date, a model may not know recent events unless it is connected to search.
Useful comparisons, and where the analogy breaks down.
A child may learn a new animal from a few pictures; many models need thousands or more.
Once trained, a model can apply its pattern millions of times quickly and consistently.
Humans connect new lessons to bodies, senses, goals and common sense. Models only have their data.

children.topic: Both can learn the wrong thing
children.note: People pick up prejudices from what they see; models do the same from their data.

manas.q: What do human and machine learning have in common when it comes to bias?

nodeData.note: AI is powerful but far from magic. This map separates common myths from reality and explains the main limits: made-up answers, bias, understanding, jobs, energy and what AI still cannot do.

children.note: Popular beliefs about AI that are wrong or badly overstated.
AI outputs are best guesses from patterns. They can be wrong while sounding completely sure.

manas.q: Is AI output always correct?

children.note: A chatbot is not a live copy of the internet. It learned patterns up to a training date and may lack recent or local facts.
AI learns from human-made data and design choices, so it can carry human biases.

manas.q: Why is AI not automatically neutral or fair?

children.note: Today's AI processes patterns in numbers. It has no body, life experience or goals of its own in the human sense.

children.topic: Myth: AI is one big brain
children.note: There are thousands of separate AI systems, each built for particular tasks by different organisations.

children.topic: Myth: AI has its own wishes
children.note: Today's systems pursue the goals people set in training and instructions. Film robots with secret plans are fiction, though experts do study future risks.
Extra data helps only if it is accurate, relevant and varied. Piling up poor data can make problems worse.

children.topic: Myth: it will soon do everything
children.note: Progress is fast in some areas and slow in others. Physical work, judgement and trust remain hard for machines.
Generative AI can produce false information that looks and sounds convincing.
When an AI states something false or invented as if it were fact, such as a fake quote, wrong date or non-existent book.

manas.q: What is an AI 'hallucination'?

children.note: Language models generate likely-sounding text one piece at a time. Plausible is not the same as true, and they may not signal when they are unsure.

manas.q: Why do chatbots make things up?

children.note: Chatbots have produced citations to papers and court cases that do not exist. Always open and check any source they give.
The writing style is equally smooth whether the content is right or wrong, so confidence is not a sign of accuracy.
Ask for sources, give the tool your own trusted documents, ask it to say when unsure, and check key facts yourself.
Methods to detect when a model is likely making things up are an active area of research, but no fix is complete.
A study proposing a way to flag likely made-up answers by checking how consistent a model's meanings are across repeats.
Does AI understand what it says, or feel anything? This is a real debate, not a settled fact.

children.topic: Fluent is not the same as understanding
children.note: A system can produce sensible-looking language without grasping meaning the way people do. How much it 'understands' is disputed.
Philosopher John Searle's 1980 thought experiment: following rules to answer in Chinese, without knowing Chinese, would not be understanding.

manas.q: What does the Chinese room argument claim?

children.note: Some researchers argue that large models do build useful internal representations of the world, a limited kind of understanding.
There is no scientific agreement that any current AI has feelings or awareness. Saying 'I feel' is a pattern of words, not proof.

manas.q: Do current AI systems have feelings?

children.note: People naturally treat things that talk as if they have minds, as early users of the 1960s ELIZA program did. This makes chatbots feel more human than they are.
If people believe AI cares about them, they may trust it too much or share too much. Treat it as a tool.
AI can treat some groups worse than others, often without anyone intending it.
From unbalanced data, past unfair decisions in the records, poor labels or a badly chosen goal.

manas.q: Where does AI bias come from?

children.note: A widely used US health algorithm used past spending as a stand-in for need, and so under-identified Black patients who were equally sick.

manas.q: How did a US health algorithm show bias?

children.note: Tools often work best in English and worst in languages with little online text, such as many African languages.
Some face and skin-image systems have performed worse on darker skin when their training photos lacked variety.
Test results separately for different groups, use varied data, explain decisions, and give people a way to challenge them.
The study that showed how a cost-based risk score disadvantaged Black patients, and how changing the goal reduced the gap.
AI changes work, but the picture is more mixed than 'robots take all jobs'.
History shows technology removes some tasks, changes many jobs and creates new ones. The mix and the speed are what worry people.

manas.q: Does AI simply wipe out jobs?

children.note: AI usually takes over parts of a job, such as drafting, sorting or summarising, while people keep the rest.
Desk work involving text, images and routine analysis is more exposed than hands-on work like plumbing, nursing or farming.
Some roles, such as basic translation, call-centre work and simple design, have seen pressure. Gains may not be shared fairly.
Data labelling, AI checking, training staff and new services built on AI create jobs, though not always well paid.
Learning to use AI well, building judgement and people skills, and checking AI output keep workers valuable.
Training and running AI uses a lot of electricity, water and hardware.
Big models run on thousands of powerful chips in data centres that need electricity and cooling, both to train and to answer questions.

manas.q: Why does AI use so much energy?

children.note: Many data centres use water to keep equipment cool, which matters in dry regions.
Making chips needs mining and factories, and old equipment becomes electronic waste.
Estimates vary widely depending on what is counted, so treat single dramatic figures with caution.

manas.q: Why are estimates of AI's energy use so different?

children.note: Chips and models are becoming more efficient per answer, but growing use can still push total energy demand up.
Pick a simpler tool when it is enough, and avoid needless repeated generation of long text, images or video.
Clear limits worth remembering when you use AI.
AI cannot be held accountable. A person or organisation remains responsible for decisions made with it.

manas.q: Who is responsible when AI is used to make a decision?

children.note: It cannot promise accuracy, especially on recent, local or specialist facts.
It does not see your patient, farm, family or business unless you tell it, and even then misses context.
It can fail at simple real-world reasoning that a child would get right, especially in unusual situations.

children.topic: Act safely in the physical world
children.note: Robots and self-driving systems still struggle with messy, unpredictable real environments.
In medicine, law and finance, AI can assist, but qualified professionals must check and decide.

manas.q: Can AI replace a doctor's or lawyer's judgement?

nodeData.note: AI is changing many jobs and creating some new ones. This map explains the main AI roles, how AI helps people in ordinary professions, the skills to build, free ways to learn, and traps to avoid.

children.note: AI mostly changes parts of jobs rather than whole jobs at once. Some tasks get faster or disappear, new tasks appear, and people who can work well alongside AI become more valuable.
Most jobs are a bundle of many tasks. AI may take over a few of them, such as drafting a letter or sorting invoices, while the rest still need a person.

manas.q: Does AI usually replace whole jobs or individual tasks?

children.note: Automation means a machine does a task instead of a person. Augmentation means the tool helps a person do the task better or faster, with the person still in charge.

manas.q: What is the difference between automation and augmentation?

children.note: This is job loss caused by new technology, like hand weavers losing work to mechanised looms. Whether such losses last long-term, or new jobs replace them, has been debated for over a century.

manas.q: What is technological unemployment?

children.note: Past waves of technology, from tractors to computers, removed some jobs and created others. The change was often painful for the workers affected, even when the overall economy grew.
A 2023 experiment found professionals given ChatGPT finished writing tasks faster and with higher rated quality. One study on one kind of task does not predict a whole economy.
A 2023 study in Science gave half of 453 professionals ChatGPT for job-like writing tasks; on average they took about 40% less time and produced better-rated work.

children.topic: No one knows the full picture
children.note: Forecasts about how many jobs AI will change vary widely. Be wary of anyone who quotes a precise number of jobs "lost" or "created" as if it were certain.
AI work is done by teams with different skills. Some roles need deep programming and maths; others mainly need careful judgement, subject knowledge or communication.
Cleans and summarises data, builds charts and dashboards, and answers business questions, for example which branches of a shop sell most. Tools: spreadsheets, SQL, sometimes Python.

manas.q: What does a data analyst mainly do?

children.note: Combines statistics, programming and subject knowledge to find patterns in data and build predictive models, such as forecasting which loan customers may fall behind.

manas.q: How is a data scientist different from a data analyst?

children.note: Turns models into reliable software that real users depend on. Needs strong programming, an understanding of how models learn, and care about speed and cost.
MLOps applies the habits of software operations to machine learning: deploying models, watching them for problems, and retraining them as data changes.

manas.q: What does MLOps stand for and do?

children.note: Builds the pipelines and databases that collect, store and move data so others can use it. Without good data plumbing, AI projects stall.
A newer title for people who build apps on top of existing large models, connecting them to company data and tools, rather than training models from scratch.
Invents and tests new methods, often with a master's degree or PhD. Works in universities and research labs and publishes papers.

manas.q: Which AI role usually needs a research degree?

children.note: Writing good instructions for AI models became a job title around 2023, but stand-alone prompt engineer roles have become less common as everyone is trained to prompt and models improve.

manas.q: Why has the prompt engineer job title become less common?

children.note: Decides what an AI product should do and for whom, balances what users need with what the technology can reliably deliver, and coordinates the team.
Checks AI systems for fairness, privacy and legal compliance, and writes rules for their use. Backgrounds in law, social science or policy are common.
People tag images, text or audio so models can learn, for example marking which pixels show a bicycle. It is an entry point, but pay and conditions vary a lot.

manas.q: What is data annotation?

children.note: Most people will not take an AI job; they will use AI inside the job they already have. Knowing your field and knowing AI's limits together is a strong combination.
AI tools can draft clinical notes, summarise records or flag possible findings on scans. The clinician must still check the output and remains responsible for the patient.

manas.q: Who stays responsible when a doctor uses an AI tool?

children.topic: 📄 Paper: AI, burnout and health workers
children.note: A 2024 review in BMJ Health & Care Informatics weighs how AI scribes and admin tools might ease burnout, against risks such as job worries and new burdens.
AI can help read receipts, match transactions and draft reports. Accountants add judgement on tax rules, unusual items and ethics that a tool cannot be trusted with alone.
Teachers can use AI to draft lesson plans, quizzes or simpler versions of a text. They still need to check facts, suit local syllabuses, and decide how students may use AI.
Phone apps can help identify crop pests from a photo or give weather and market information. Advice should be checked with local extension officers who know the area.
AI can summarise documents and draft letters, but it may invent cases or rules. Every citation and figure must be checked against the official source.
A shop or salon owner might use AI to write adverts, reply to customers or plan stock. The value comes from knowing your customers, which the tool does not.
Different roles need different mixes, but a few skills help almost everyone. Technical skills can be learned step by step; judgement and communication matter at every level.
Knowing what AI can and cannot do, how it makes mistakes, and when to trust or double-check it. This is the base skill for everyone, not just specialists.

manas.q: What is AI literacy?

children.note: Being comfortable reading tables and charts, asking where data came from, and spotting when numbers are misleading or incomplete.
Spreadsheets are the everyday tool for data in most offices. SQL is the common language for asking questions of databases and is key for analyst roles.
Python is the most widely used language in data science and machine learning. Technical roles expect it; non-technical users can go far without it.

manas.q: Which programming language is most common in AI work?

children.note: Understanding averages, variation, samples and uncertainty helps you judge whether a pattern is real or chance. It sits at the heart of machine learning.
Deep knowledge of a field such as health, farming or banking lets you ask the right questions and spot when an AI answer makes no sense.

manas.q: Why is domain knowledge valuable in AI work?

children.note: Explaining results in plain language to managers, patients or customers is often what makes AI work useful. Clear writing is a career skill in itself.
Asking who could be harmed, whether data is biased, and whether a result is believable protects people and your own reputation.
You do not need to pay a lot to start. Pick a path that fits your goal and finish one course before starting the next.
For managers, professionals and students who want understanding, not coding. Start with a non-technical course, then practise using AI tools in your own work.
A free online course from the University of Helsinki, first launched in 2018, for non-experts. It covers what AI is, machine learning basics and AI's effect on society.

manas.q: Which free course from the University of Helsinki introduces AI to non-experts?

children.note: Learn spreadsheets, then SQL, then basic statistics and charts, and finally some Python. Practise on public data from your own country or sector.
Learn Python and basic statistics first, then a practical machine learning course, then build and share a few projects of your own.
A free, self-paced introduction to machine learning from Google with short lessons and exercises.
A free course by the non-profit fast.ai, founded in 2016, that teaches deep learning hands-on. Its only stated requirement is some Python.

manas.q: What does fast.ai's course expect you to know beforehand?

children.note: Free courses on working with modern language and image models using the Hugging Face tools and model-sharing platform.
Offers many short courses and longer specialisations on machine learning and generative AI; several short courses are free.
Thirty to sixty minutes a day, every day, beats an occasional long weekend. Keep notes and redo exercises without looking at the answers.
Employers want to see what you can do, not only what certificates you hold. A small set of real, well-explained projects is your best evidence.
Analyse data you understand, such as rainfall and maize yields, clinic waiting times, or matatu or bus routes. Local problems make you stand out.

manas.q: What makes a portfolio project stand out?

children.note: Kaggle is a Google-owned platform with public datasets, online notebooks and data science competitions. It is a good place to practise and learn from others' code.

manas.q: What is Kaggle?

children.note: GitHub is a site for storing and sharing code. A tidy profile with clear project descriptions shows employers how you work.
Short blog posts or LinkedIn articles explaining a project in plain words show communication skill and help others find you.
Three finished projects with clear goals, honest limits and readable results are worth more than twenty copied tutorials.
Explain what problem you chose, why, what went wrong and what you would do next. Employers value judgement as much as accuracy scores.
AI jobs are found through a mix of local employers, remote work and community connections. Start where you are, with the skills and network you already have.
Often the easiest step is to use AI and data skills in your present role, for example automating a monthly report, then take on bigger projects.
Many data and AI tasks can be done online for clients anywhere. Competition is global, so a strong portfolio and reliable delivery matter.

manas.q: Why does a portfolio matter so much for remote work?

children.note: Data science and AI communities run meetups, study groups and hackathons in cities such as Nairobi, Lagos, Bengaluru and many others. They help you learn and hear about jobs.
Internships, industrial attachments and volunteer data projects with NGOs or hospitals give real experience. Check that any programme is genuine before applying.
Kenya and India have become centres for AI data-labelling work. It can be a first step, but reports have raised concerns about low pay and distressing content, so read contracts carefully.
Titles vary a lot between companies. Read the list of tasks and tools in an advert to understand what the job really involves.
The AI boom attracts scams and shortcuts. Knowing the common traps protects your money, your data and your reputation.
Be suspicious of offers that ask you to pay a fee for training, equipment or registration before you can start "AI work", or promise high pay for little effort.

manas.q: What is a warning sign of an AI job scam?

children.note: Do not send ID copies, bank details or mobile money PINs to unknown recruiters. Real employers verify you through proper, traceable channels.
A certificate shows you finished a course, not that you can do the work. Employers usually test skills directly or ask about your projects.

manas.q: Why is a certificate alone not enough?

children.note: If AI writes all your code or reports, you may not learn the skill yourself and may miss its errors. Use it to learn faster, not to skip learning.
Job titles rise and fall quickly, as prompt engineer showed. Lasting basics such as data skills, statistics and domain knowledge age much better.
Using patient, client or customer data carelessly can break laws such as Kenya's Data Protection Act and damage trust. Check the rules before you start.
